description: We are SolutionX team, with two software engineers passionate about space exploration. We love turning complex data into simple, useful tools, and we want to build technology that helps astronauts and mission teams make faster, safer decisions. We combine skills in software development, data analysis and design, and we enjoy solving real problems as a team. Our team is complete, and we’re excited to create something meaningful for NASA Space Apps 2026!
summary:
LunaWindow is a web-based mission planner that shows when a lunar landing site has sunlight for solar power and a direct radio link to Earth. At the Moon's south pole the Sun stays only a few degrees above the horizon, crater rims cast shadows tens of kilometres long, and Earth can slip below the skyline, so a site that looks good on a map can leave a lander without power or contact.

For any site and date, LunaWindow computes Sun and Earth positions from NASA/JPL ephemerides and lunar orientation kernels, then traces 1,440 rays across real NASA LRO LOLA terrain to find the true horizon. The results appear as a 3D view of the site, a clear GO/CAUTION/NO-GO verdict, an operations timeline and a side-by-side comparison of sites. A 12-month calendar finds the best landing dates, a battery simulator shows whether a lander survives the lunar night, and an AI Mission Copilot answers questions using LunaWindow's own calculations.

Our Sun positions match JPL Horizons to within 0.03 arcseconds. LunaWindow turns hours of expert analysis into seconds, helping teams choose safer sites and react quickly when a launch date slips.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LunaWindow answers a question every lunar mission must answer before landing: when will this site have sunlight for solar power, and when will it have a direct line of sight to Earth for radio contact? At the lunar south pole, the target of upcoming Artemis and commercial missions, the Sun stays a few degrees above the horizon, crater rims and mountains cast shadows tens of kilometres long, and Earth can drop below the skyline. A site that looks good on a map can leave a lander without power or contact.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Sky positions: for any site and date range, we compute where the Sun and Earth appear in the local sky, using the NASA/JPL DE421 ephemeris and NAIF lunar orientation kernels (Moon mean-Earth frame) through the Skyfield library.

2. Real horizon: for sites in the polar region (75°S–90°S) we read NASA's LRO LOLA 240 m elevation map and trace 1,440 rays out to 200 km in every direction, including lunar curvature. This gives the true skyline angle around the site.

3. Visibility: the Sun counts as "up" while any part of its disc clears the real skyline, and Earth while it is above it. The result, hour by hour, is when the lander has power, has a link, or has both.

WHAT THE USER SEES

- A 3D view of 50 x 50 km of real LOLA terrain around the site, lit by the computed Sun, with a time scrubber. There is also a whole-Moon globe view.

- A plain GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict, with % time with power, % time with an Earth link, the longest night and the longest communication blackout.

- A 360° horizon view, an operations timeline and Sun/Earth elevation charts.

- Launch-slip buttons (-7, +7, +14 days) and a side-by-side comparison of candidate sites.

- Best Landing Window: scores a landing on every day of the next 12 months and marks the best dates on a colour calendar.

- Night survival simulator: an hour-by-hour battery model (panel power, battery size, day and night loads). It shows whether the lander survives, the exact hour the battery would run out, and the smallest battery that would survive.

- Mission Copilot: an AI assistant (Google Gemini) that answers plain-language questions by calling LunaWindow's own calculation tools instead of answering from memory. It offers one-click "Open in planner" buttons.

EXAMPLE

At the IM-1 Odysseus landing site, landing on 15 March 2027 for 14 days gets a GO verdict, with 78% sunlight. But the lander touches down at local night, and a small lander with a 2 kWh battery runs out of power within the first day. The calendar finds 8 November 2027 instead: power and an Earth link for 91% of the mission, and the same lander survives.

ACCURACY AND VALIDATION

- Sun positions match NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.03 arcseconds.

- The floor of Shackleton crater shows 0% sunlight for all of 2027, as expected for a permanently shadowed region.

- Terrain matters: at the IM-1 site, a flat horizon gives 49.5% sunlight over 2027, while the real LOLA horizon gives 38.6%. Ignoring terrain overstates sunlight by more than a quarter.

- Every NASA data file is checked against a SHA-256 fingerprint before use.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Turns hours of expert work with ephemeris and terrain tools into an answer in seconds.

- Lets teams re-plan immediately when a launch slips, which happens often.

- Helps avoid sites and dates that leave a lander dark or out of contact, which can end a mission.

- Is open to students, educators and the public, not only specialists, with a clear verdict and an assistant that explains results in plain words.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Skyfield, NumPy.

- NASA data: JPL DE421 ephemeris, NAIF lunar orientation and frame kernels (moon_pa_de421, moon_080317.tf, pck00008.tpc), LRO LOLA LDEM_75S_240M.

- Frontend: React 18, Vite, Three.js for the 3D terrain and globe, SVG charts.

- AI: Google Gemini API with function calling.

- Cloud: Microsoft Azure App Service (API) and Azure Static Web Apps (website).

- CI/CD: GitHub Actions deploys automatically on every push.

- Hardware: none. It runs in any modern web browser, on desktop or phone.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- It turns a technical calculation into a mission decision: a verdict, a best date and a survival check, not just numbers.

- The lander loading animation shows the real calculation steps as they finish.

- The AI copilot is grounded: it cannot invent numbers, because every figure comes from our NASA-based tools.

- An interactive scroll story explains the problem to non-experts before they use the tool.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy over appearance: real ephemerides and real terrain, checked against NASA JPL Horizons.

- Honesty about limits: the battery model is simplified (no panel tilt, temperature or ageing). Outside the LOLA polar map the horizon is flat. Communication is direct-to-Earth only, without relay satellites. One site's coordinates are marked as approximate in the app.

- Valid date range 1950–2049, set by the DE421 ephemeris.

- Speed: terrain horizons are cached, so later requests are fast.

- Cost and access: runs on free cloud tiers, protects the free AI quota with rate limits, and works on phones.

DEMO VIDEO

Watch LunaWindow in action. The video shows the problem at the lunar south pole, then a walkthrough of the live planner: the 3D terrain view and verdict, the 12-month best landing window, the night survival battery check, and the Mission Copilot answering a question and opening the plan in one click. Everything in the video is recorded from the real, working website.
